section.title: Sennacherib Threatens Jerusalem
section.sectionRationale: This narrative opens the Hezekiah interlude, chapters 36 to 39, a historical pause between the oracles of judgment and the Book of Comfort. Assyria's field commander mocks Judah's trust in Egypt and in the LORD alike, but Hezekiah takes the blasphemous letter straight to the temple and to prayer, and the LORD alone, without a single Judean sword raised, destroys the army besieging His city and strikes down the boastful king himself.
section.thesis: When Assyria's spokesman taunts Jerusalem with the question 'How can the LORD deliver you?', King Hezekiah answers not with defiance or despair but with prayer, and the LORD vindicates His own name before all the kingdoms of the earth by destroying the Assyrian army untouched by human hands, for the sake of His own glory and His promise to David.
section.frameNote: Six scenes: the Rabshakeh's public threat outside Jerusalem's walls; his psychological warfare aimed at the people on the wall; Hezekiah's mourning and Isaiah's first word of assurance; Sennacherib's letter and Hezekiah's prayer in the temple; the LORD's answer through Isaiah, taunting the king of Assyria in turn; and the angel of the LORD striking down the Assyrian camp.

units.label: The Rabshakeh's public threat
units.note: trusting in Egypt, trusting in the LORD

verses.text: In the fourteenth year of Hezekiah's reign, Sennacherib king of Assyria attacked and captured all the fortified cities of Judah.
And the king of Assyria sent the Rabshakeh, with a great army, from Lachish to King Hezekiah at Jerusalem. And he stopped by the aqueduct of the upper pool, on the road to the Launderer's Field.
Then Eliakim son of Hilkiah the palace administrator, Shebna the scribe, and Joah son of Asaph the recorder, went out to him.
The Rabshakeh said to them, “Tell Hezekiah that this is what the great king, the king of Assyria, says: What is the basis of this confidence of yours?
You claim to have a strategy and strength for war, but these are empty words. In whom are you now trusting, that you have rebelled against me?
Look now, you are trusting in Egypt, that splintered reed of a staff that will pierce the hand of anyone who leans on it. Such is Pharaoh king of Egypt to all who trust in him.

But if you say to me, ‘We {{batach|trust}} in the LORD our God,’ is He not the One whose high places and altars Hezekiah has removed, saying to Judah and Jerusalem, ‘You must worship before this altar’?
Now, therefore, make a bargain with my master, the king of Assyria. I will give you two thousand horses, if you can put riders on them!
For how can you repel a single officer among the least of my master's servants when you depend on Egypt for chariots and horsemen?
So now, was it apart from the LORD that I have come up against this land to destroy it? The LORD Himself said to me, ‘Go up against this land and destroy it.’”

units.label: Psychological warfare on the wall
units.note: do not let Hezekiah deceive you

verses.text: Then Eliakim, Shebna, and Joah said to the Rabshakeh, “Please speak to your servants in Aramaic, since we understand it. Do not speak to us in Hebrew in the hearing of the people on the wall.”

But the Rabshakeh replied, “Has my master sent me to speak these words only to you and your master, and not to the men sitting on the wall, who are destined with you to eat their own dung and drink their own urine?”
Then the Rabshakeh stood and called out loudly in Hebrew: “Hear the words of the great king, the king of Assyria!
This is what the king says: Do not let Hezekiah deceive you, for he cannot deliver you.
Do not let Hezekiah persuade you to trust in the LORD when he says, ‘The LORD will surely deliver us; this city will not be given into the hand of the king of Assyria.’

Do not listen to Hezekiah, for this is what the king of Assyria says: Make peace with me and come out to me. Then every one of you will eat from his own vine and his own fig tree, and drink water from his own cistern,
until I come and take you away to a land like your own, a land of grain and new wine, a land of bread and vineyards.
Do not let Hezekiah mislead you when he says, ‘The LORD will deliver us.’ Has the god of any nation ever delivered his land from the hand of the king of Assyria?
Where are the gods of Hamath and Arpad? Where are the gods of Sepharvaim? Have they delivered Samaria from my hand?
Who among all the gods of these lands has delivered his land from my hand? How then can the LORD deliver Jerusalem from my hand?”
But the people remained silent and did not answer a word, for Hezekiah had commanded, “Do not answer him.”
Then Hilkiah's son Eliakim the palace administrator, Shebna the scribe, and Asaph's son Joah the recorder came to Hezekiah with their clothes torn, and they relayed to him the words of the Rabshakeh.

units.label: Hezekiah's mourning and Isaiah's word
units.note: lift up a prayer for the remnant

verses.text: On hearing this report, King Hezekiah tore his clothes, put on sackcloth, and entered the house of the LORD.
And he sent Eliakim the palace administrator, Shebna the scribe, and the leading priests, all wearing sackcloth, to the prophet Isaiah son of Amoz
to tell him, “This is what Hezekiah says: Today is a day of distress, rebuke, and disgrace; for children have come to the point of birth, but there is no strength to deliver them.

Perhaps the LORD your God will hear the words of the Rabshakeh, whom his master the king of Assyria has sent to {{charaph|defy}} the living God, and He will rebuke him for the words that the LORD your God has heard. Therefore lift up a prayer for the remnant that still survives.”
So the servants of King Hezekiah went to Isaiah,
who replied, “Tell your master that this is what the LORD says: ‘Do not be afraid of the words you have heard, with which the servants of the king of Assyria have blasphemed Me.
Behold, I will put a spirit in him so that he will hear a rumor and return to his own land, where I will cause him to fall by the sword.’”
When the Rabshakeh heard that the king of Assyria had left Lachish, he withdrew and found the king fighting against Libnah.
Now Sennacherib had been warned about Tirhakah king of Cush: “He has set out to fight against you.” On hearing this, Sennacherib sent messengers to Hezekiah, saying,
“Give this message to Hezekiah king of Judah: ‘Do not let your God, in whom you trust, deceive you by saying that Jerusalem will not be delivered into the hand of the king of Assyria.
Surely you have heard what the kings of Assyria have done to all the other countries, devoting them to destruction. Will you then be spared?
Did the gods of the nations destroyed by my fathers rescue those nations, the gods of Gozan, Haran, and Rezeph, and of the people of Eden in Telassar?
Where are the kings of Hamath, Arpad, Sepharvaim, Hena, and Ivvah?’”
So Hezekiah received the letter from the messengers, read it, and went up to the house of the LORD and spread it out before the LORD.
And Hezekiah prayed to the LORD:
“O LORD of Hosts, God of Israel, enthroned above the cherubim, You alone are God over all the kingdoms of the earth. You made the heavens and the earth.
Incline Your ear, O LORD, and hear; open Your eyes, O LORD, and see. Listen to all the words that Sennacherib has sent to defy the living God.
Truly, O LORD, the kings of Assyria have laid waste all these countries and their lands.
They have cast their gods into the fire and destroyed them, for they were not gods, but only wood and stone, the work of human hands.
And now, O LORD our God, save us from his hand, so that all the kingdoms of the earth may know that You alone, O LORD, are God.”

units.label: The LORD's answer through Isaiah
units.note: the zeal of the LORD will accomplish this

verses.text: Then Isaiah son of Amoz sent a message to Hezekiah: “This is what the LORD, the God of Israel, says: Because you have prayed to Me concerning Sennacherib king of Assyria,
this is the word that the LORD has spoken against him: ‘The Virgin Daughter of Zion despises you and mocks you; the Daughter of Jerusalem shakes her head behind you.
Whom have you taunted and {{charaph|blasphemed}}? Against whom have you raised your voice and lifted your eyes in pride? Against the Holy One of Israel!

Through your servants you have taunted the Lord, and you have said: “With my many chariots I have ascended to the heights of the mountains, to the remote peaks of Lebanon. I have cut down its tallest cedars, the finest of its cypresses. I have reached its farthest heights, the densest of its forests.
I have dug wells and drunk foreign waters. With the soles of my feet I have dried up all the streams of Egypt.”
Have you not heard? Long ago I ordained it; in days of old I planned it. Now I have brought it to pass, that you should crush fortified cities into piles of rubble.
Therefore their inhabitants, devoid of power, are dismayed and ashamed. They are like plants in the field, tender green shoots, grass on the rooftops, scorched before it is grown.
But I know your sitting down, your going out and coming in, and your raging against Me.
Because your rage and arrogance against Me have reached My ears, I will put My hook in your nose and My bit in your mouth; I will send you back the way you came.’

And this will be a sign to you, O Hezekiah: This year you will eat what grows on its own, and in the second year what springs from the same. But in the third year you will sow and reap; you will plant vineyards and eat their fruit.
And the surviving remnant of the house of Judah will again take root below and bear fruit above.
For a remnant will go forth from Jerusalem, and survivors from Mount Zion. The zeal of the LORD of Hosts will accomplish this.
So this is what the LORD says about the king of Assyria: ‘He will not enter this city or shoot an arrow into it. He will not come before it with a shield or build up a siege ramp against it.
He will go back the way he came, and he will not enter this city,’ declares the LORD.
‘I will defend this city and save it for My own sake and for the sake of My servant David.’”

units.label: The angel of the LORD strikes

verses.text: Then the angel of the LORD went out and struck down 185,000 men in the camp of the Assyrians. When the people got up the next morning, there were all the dead bodies!
So Sennacherib king of Assyria broke camp and withdrew. He returned to Nineveh and stayed there.

One day, while he was worshiping in the temple of his god Nisroch, his sons Adrammelech and Sharezer put him to the sword and escaped to the land of Ararat. And his son Esar-haddon reigned in his place.

batach.gloss: To trust, to lean one's full weight on someone or something with confidence. The Rabshakeh mocks Judah's trust in Egypt as leaning on a splintered reed, then twists the very word Judah would use of the LORD, exposing that the real question of the whole narrative is not military strategy but where trust ultimately rests.

charaph.gloss: To defy, taunt, or blaspheme, to hurl scorn at someone as though they were beneath notice. Sennacherib's servants use this word against the living God Himself, and the LORD's answering oracle in chapter 37 throws the same word back at the king, promising that whoever taunts the Holy One of Israel will himself be brought low.

basic.context: Assyria's king Sennacherib has swept through Judah's fortified cities and now sends his field commander, the Rabshakeh, to demand Jerusalem's surrender. In blistering public speech he mocks Judah's trust in Egypt and in the LORD alike, asking how any god could deliver a city from Assyria's hand. King Hezekiah, rather than answering in kind, tears his clothes, goes to the temple, and sends for the prophet Isaiah, and eventually spreads the enemy's own letter out before the LORD in prayer.
basic.hermeneutics: This is a real historical event, corroborated in outline by 2 Kings 18 to 19, 2 Chronicles 32, and Assyrian records that, tellingly, never claim to have captured Jerusalem itself. The narrative's theological center is not military strategy but the question the Rabshakeh keeps raising, on whom does Judah's trust really rest, and the LORD answers by acting entirely without human military help, striking down the Assyrian army and vindicating His own name.
basic.originalLanguages: The Rabshakeh's whole speech circles the word {{batach}}, trust, mocking Egypt as a splintered reed and twisting even the language of trusting the LORD into an accusation. His masters' messengers go further, using the word {{charaph}}, to defy or blaspheme, against the living God Himself, language the LORD's own answering oracle in chapter 37 turns directly back upon the king of Assyria.
basic.typology: Hezekiah's response, taking a blasphemous threat and laying it open before God in prayer rather than answering in his own strength, anticipates the pattern of every believer's access to God through intercession, and points toward Christ, the greater Son of David for whose sake, alongside His own name, the LORD says He will defend the city, verse 35. The angel of the LORD striking down an army without a human hand raised anticipates the pattern of salvation that is God's work alone, not human achievement.
basic.christ: The LORD explicitly says He will save Jerusalem 'for My own sake and for the sake of My servant David,' verse 35, tying this deliverance to the Davidic covenant that runs forward to Christ, the Son of David, Matthew 1:1. Hezekiah's prayer, taking the enemy's taunting letter and laying it before God rather than trusting his own resources, models the access to the Father that believers now have boldly through Christ, our great High Priest, Hebrews 4:14-16.
basic.god: God alone delivers Jerusalem, without so much as an arrow shot by Judah, so that, as Hezekiah prays, all the kingdoms of the earth may know that the LORD alone is God. He hears and answers prayer even when His own name has been openly blasphemed, and He acts both for His own glory and out of covenant faithfulness to His promise to David.
basic.crossReferences: 2 Kings 18:13-19:37 and 2 Chronicles 32:1-23 record the same events. Psalm 46 is traditionally associated with this deliverance, celebrating God as a very present help in trouble. Hebrews 4:14-16 invites believers to approach God's throne boldly, as Hezekiah brought his crisis directly to the LORD. Matthew 1:1 traces Christ's lineage to David, for whose sake the LORD defends Jerusalem here.
basic.oneStory: This narrative shows a king who, when mocked and threatened beyond his own strength, brings the crisis to God in prayer rather than trusting alliances or despair, and a God who answers by acting alone, for His own name and for the sake of His covenant with David. It is a preview of the greater deliverance God works through David's greatest Son, Christ, who saves His people not by their strength but by His own.

context.literary:
Isaiah 36 and 37 are a single narrative, and they are written as a drama in three rounds. In the first, the Rabshakeh speaks, chapter 36, and the king is silent. In the second, a letter arrives and Hezekiah answers it in prayer, 37:8 to 20. In the third, the LORD answers through Isaiah, with a poem of taunt and a sign, and then with an act, 37:21 to 38. Each round is built on the same word, 'hear,' and on the same question, who is truly God. The Rabshakeh says 'Hear the words of the great king,' 36:13; Hezekiah says 'Listen to all the words that Sennacherib has sent,' 37:17; and the LORD says 'Have you not heard? Long ago I ordained it,' 37:26.

The story is also arranged as a series of exchanges between the visible and the hidden. The Assyrian stands in public, with an army, in the language of the street. Hezekiah goes into the house of the LORD in sackcloth, out of sight. In the first round the words are all on the wall; in the last the action is all in the camp, in the night, with the angel. The reader is made to feel that the real contest is happening where the Assyrian cannot see.

The pairs of names matter too. Eliakim, Shebna and Joah appear in the same order before and after the speeches, 36:3 and 36:22, as if the narrator wanted us to watch the same three men go out confident and come back with torn clothes. The chapter ends with a cold irony: Sennacherib dies in a temple, killed by his own sons in front of the god he worshipped, 37:38.
context.historical:
The invasion took place in 701 BC, the fourteenth year of Hezekiah, 36:1. Hezekiah had rebelled against Assyria and had prepared for a siege, 2 Chronicles 32:1 to 8, including the tunnel that brought water into the city, 2 Kings 20:20. Sennacherib's campaign took the walled cities of Judah one by one, and Lachish, the most important of them, was where he set up his headquarters, 36:2. The Assyrian palace at Nineveh later displayed carved reliefs of the siege of Lachish, and Sennacherib's own annals boast of shutting Hezekiah up in Jerusalem like a bird in a cage. They do not claim to have taken the city, which fits the biblical story.

Isaiah's version leaves out the tribute that Hezekiah sent, which 2 Kings 18:14 to 16 records. It gives the reader the part of the story that matters theologically: the city that Assyria could not take. The Rabshakeh, whose title means a high officer, spoke where he did for a reason. The 'aqueduct of the upper pool, on the road to the Launderer's Field' is the very place where Isaiah had met Ahaz thirty or more years earlier and told him not to fear, 7:3. The same ground, the same water, a new king.

The Rabshakeh's use of Hebrew, or 'the dialect of Judah' as the BSB footnote has it, was deliberate propaganda. Aramaic was the language of diplomacy, and Judah's officials asked him to use it so that the ordinary people would not understand. He refused and spoke to the wall. Eliakim and Shebna are the same two officials of the palace whose fortunes Isaiah described in 22:15 to 25, with Shebna now serving as scribe.
context.canonical:
Isaiah 36 to 39 forms a historical hinge in the book. These four chapters are drawn almost word for word from 2 Kings 18:13 to 20:19, and they connect the first half of Isaiah, with its warnings of Assyria, to the second half, with its comfort for Babylon's exiles. The first half ends with Assyria defeated and Zion kept. The last chapter of the section ends with Babylon's envoys admiring Hezekiah's treasures and Isaiah saying that one day everything would go there, 39:6. So the story is both a vindication and a warning.

The deliverance was remembered in Israel's songs. Psalms 46, 48 and 76 speak of God as a refuge, of kings who gather against Zion and flee, of weapons broken and a city that does not fall, and many readers connect them with this event. The Chronicler tells the story with an emphasis on Hezekiah's prayer and on the reward of trust, 2 Chronicles 32:20 to 23.

The angel who strikes in the night recalls the Passover, when the destroyer went through Egypt and the people rose in the morning to find the dead, Exodus 12:29 to 30, and the plague of David's census, when the angel stretched out his hand over Jerusalem and was stopped, 2 Samuel 24:15 to 16. In the New Testament, the promise that the gates of Hades will not overcome the church, Matthew 16:18, and the confidence of Paul that nothing can separate us from God's love, Romans 8:31 to 39, belong to the same line of trust in a God who defends His own.

hermeneutics.authorIntent:
The narrator wanted his hearers to see two kinds of kings and two kinds of trust. The Assyrian king boasts in his own strength and counts the gods of other nations as just so many names on a list. Hezekiah, who has made mistakes, brings the whole matter to the LORD. The reader is meant to ask which of the two they resemble when they are cornered.

He also meant to show that the Rabshakeh's rhetoric is cunning. It mixes truth and lies. It is true that Egypt is a broken reed, 36:6, and that Isaiah himself had said so. It is true that the Assyrians have crushed the kingdoms he names. It is false that the LORD is one god among them, and it is a pious lie that the LORD had sent him, 36:10. The account teaches readers to listen to the argument and notice where it twists God's own words.

Finally, the narrator wants to place the deliverance firmly in God's hands. There is no battle. The Judahites do not fire an arrow, 37:33. The point is that salvation is the LORD's work, and that He does it for His own name's sake and for David's, 37:35. Anyone who finishes this narrative should have no doubt about who saved Jerusalem.
hermeneutics.descriptionVsPrescription:
The narrative records what Hezekiah did, and it commends him, but it does not turn every detail into a command. Hezekiah's tearing of his clothes, his sackcloth, and his spreading the letter in the temple were a king's response in a crisis, and the story gives no instruction that believers must lay physical letters before God. What it commends is the direction of his action: toward the LORD, with the problem in full view and no pretense.

It also does not promise that every city under threat will be spared. Other cities in Israel's history fell, and Samaria had fallen just twenty years earlier, 2 Kings 17. The promise here is tied to a particular word from the LORD, spoken through Isaiah, and to the covenant with David. Believers cannot treat it as a guarantee that a sincere prayer will always turn back an invader.

What carries forward is the pattern: honest prayer in the face of threat, trust in the character of God more than in alliances, and the readiness to hear a word from Him through Scripture. Philippians 4:6 to 7 asks believers to bring everything to God in prayer, and 1 Peter 5:7 tells them to cast their anxieties on Him. That is Hezekiah's gesture with the letter, generalised.

debates.question: Did Sennacherib invade Judah once or twice, and how does the tribute of 2 Kings 18:14 to 16 fit with the deliverance?

views.label: One campaign in 701 BC
views.case: The Assyrian records and the biblical record describe one great campaign. On this view Hezekiah first paid tribute, and Sennacherib broke the agreement and sent the Rabshakeh anyway, which is the treachery of Isaiah 33:1. The later death of Sennacherib in 681 BC, 37:38, is simply reported at the end as the outcome.

views.label: Two campaigns
views.case: Some scholars point to Tirhakah, 37:9, who was not yet king of Egypt in 701 BC, and propose a later Assyrian campaign around 690 BC in which the deliverance took place. This would separate the tribute of 701 from the angel's strike.

debates.bearing: The Bible does not state a date for the angel's strike. Tirhakah may be called 'king' in 37:9 by the narrator's later usage, as a man is often named by his later title, and the one-campaign reading is simple. Either view leaves the theology unchanged: the LORD delivered the city, and Sennacherib did not take it.

debates.question: What was the angel's strike, in historical terms?

views.label: A direct miracle
views.case: The text says the angel of the LORD went out and struck down 185,000, and the people rose in the morning to find the bodies, 37:36. This is described as divine action in the night, with no human means.

views.label: A plague or similar sudden disaster used by God
views.case: Some suggest an epidemic in the camp, noting that the Greek historian Herodotus reports a different story of Assyrian forces undone by mice in Egypt, which is sometimes read as a plague. Such a reading fits the way Scripture elsewhere describes God using pestilence, 2 Samuel 24:15, while still attributing the act to Him.

debates.bearing: The biblical writers do not describe the mechanism and do not need to. In either case the timing, the scale and the way it fulfilled Isaiah's word make it the LORD's act. The point of the narrative is not how the army died but who it was that struck.

study.originalLanguages:
The root of the whole passage is batach, 'to trust,' and the Rabshakeh uses it again and again in chapter 36. The verb describes the posture of someone who leans their full weight on something, and the Rabshakeh picks his target carefully: 'In whom are you now trusting?' 36:5. His image of Egypt as a splintered reed that pierces the hand of the one who leans on it makes the verb physical. Anyone who has leaned on such a staff knows what he means. He then turns the verb on the LORD, warning the wall not to be persuaded to 'trust' in Him, 36:15, which shows how the enemy tries to turn faith into foolishness.

The title 'the great king,' melek hagadol, is the formal title of the Assyrian emperor, used in the treaties by which Assyria bound its vassals. By using it, the Rabshakeh speaks the language of a suzerain addressing a disloyal subject. His offer in 36:8 is framed as a bargain, a trade between equals, which is mocking, since he goes on to say how few riders Judah could muster.

In 36:16 the BSB says 'Make peace with me,' with a footnote 'Make a blessing with me.' The Hebrew uses the word for blessing, berakhah. It is an unusual way of describing a surrender, and it makes the Rabshakeh sound like a rival giver of blessing. The promise that follows, each person eating from his own vine and fig tree, is the vocabulary of the peace of Solomon's day, 1 Kings 4:25, and Micah 4:4. The Assyrian offers a counterfeit of covenant blessing, and then, 'until I come and take you away,' reveals that it is an exile.

The verb in 37:4, 17 and 23 is charaph, 'to taunt, to defy, to blaspheme.' It is applied to the Rabshakeh in 37:4, to Sennacherib's letter in 37:17, and in 37:23 the LORD asks the king, 'Whom have you taunted and blasphemed?' The same word comes back on the speaker. The enemy defames the living God, and the living God asks him to name the person he thinks he insulted. The designation 'the living God' itself contrasts with the Assyrians' list of gods that are only 'wood and stone,' 37:19.

In 37:16 Hezekiah calls the LORD the one 'enthroned above the cherubim.' The phrase points to the ark of the covenant, where the LORD was said to sit above the cherubim, 1 Samuel 4:4. It places the prayer in the sanctuary, with the God who is both king of the earth and present with His people. The BSB footnote at verse 20 notes that the Dead Sea Scrolls and 2 Kings 19:19 read 'You alone are God,' where the later Hebrew text reads 'You alone are the LORD.' Either way, the content is the confession of Isaiah 43:10 to 11 and 45:5.

Verse 29 uses the image of a hook in the nose and a bit in the mouth. The Assyrians themselves led captives by hooks and rings, and the carved reliefs show it. The LORD turns the practice back on the king. In verse 32 the 'zeal' of the LORD of Hosts is qinah, the same word used in 9:7 for the force that will establish the throne of David, so that the deliverance is tied to the promise of the coming child.

typology.type: Hezekiah spreading the letter before the LORD, 37:14
typology.fulfillment: A king takes a hostile document into the sanctuary and lays it open, as a man might lay a case before a judge. The gesture anticipates the access that believers have now in Christ. Hebrews says we have a great High Priest who has passed through the heavens and invites us to approach the throne of grace with confidence, Hebrews 4:14 to 16. Paul says that in everything, by prayer and petition with thanksgiving, we are to make our requests known to God, Philippians 4:6. The type falls short in that Hezekiah's access depended on the temple and on his office as king; in Christ every believer comes through the one mediator, 1 Timothy 2:5, who Himself prays for us.

The LORD saves the city 'for the sake of My servant David.' Hezekiah is the king in David's line who prays and is answered, and his deliverance depends on a promise made to his ancestor. The correspondence points ahead to the greater Son of David, Matthew 1:1, through whom the covenant promise is fully kept. The escalation is that Hezekiah's rescue is temporary, since the city later falls to Babylon, while Christ's reign has no end, Luke 1:32 to 33. The type falls short of Christ by the king's own failings in the next chapters, 39:1 to 8, which show that Hezekiah was not the promised ruler.

typology.type: The angel who strikes the camp, 37:36
typology.fulfillment: The rescue comes not by Judah's army but by the LORD's messenger in the night, and the people wake to find the enemy dead. The shape is that of the Passover, Exodus 12:29 to 30, and it points to the way God saves: by His own act, for a people who contribute nothing. Paul describes the same pattern in Colossians 2:15, where Christ disarms the powers and rulers on the cross, triumphing over them. The type falls short in that the Assyrian army was a political and military enemy, while the enemies Christ defeated are sin, death and the devil, Hebrews 2:14 to 15.

typology.type: The remnant sign of the third year, 37:30 to 32
typology.fulfillment: For two years the people will live off what grows by itself, and in the third they will sow and reap, and the survivors 'will again take root below and bear fruit above.' It describes a remnant restored by the zeal of the LORD. The pattern is that of a seed falling and rising, and in the New Testament Jesus uses a grain of wheat that dies to bear much fruit, John 12:24, and rises on the third day, 1 Corinthians 15:4. The type falls short in that Judah's rebirth was a return of a people to their fields, while Christ's rising is the firstfruits of a new creation, 1 Corinthians 15:20.

study.christ:
The most direct line from this narrative to Christ runs through verse 35: 'I will defend this city and save it for My own sake and for the sake of My servant David.' Everything that follows in the Old Testament for the house of David hangs on that kind of promise. The deliverance of Jerusalem was not earned by Hezekiah, who was a good king with serious flaws. It was given because of a covenant that God had made with David, 2 Samuel 7:12 to 16, and that covenant looked toward a descendant whose throne would last. Matthew opens his Gospel with 'the Son of David,' 1:1, and the angel tells Mary that the Lord God will give her son the throne of His father David, Luke 1:32 to 33. The Assyrian crisis shows that God keeps the Davidic promise even when the king in David's line is weak, and the Gospels show that He kept it to the full.

Hezekiah himself is a signpost for the better king. He does what a good king does: he takes the threat to the LORD, he humbles himself, he asks the prophet to pray. His prayer is an act of faith in 'the living God,' and the LORD answers in a way that makes plain who is the real king of Jerusalem. Yet Hezekiah is also limited. Chapter 39 shows him show off his treasury to Babylon, and he is content that peace and truth will last in his days. The people need a king who does more than survive a siege. They need one who deals with the root of the problem. Christ is that king.

The Rabshakeh's question, 'How then can the LORD deliver Jerusalem from my hand?' has a last answer in Christ. The Assyrian lists the gods of the nations that were not able to save them. Paul writes that God has exalted Jesus to the highest place and given Him the name above every name, so that at the name of Jesus every knee will bow, Philippians 2:9 to 11. That is the answer to every boast like that of Sennacherib, and Hezekiah's prayer that all the kingdoms of the earth 'may know that You alone, O LORD, are God' is, in the end, answered by the confession of the nations in Jesus' name.

There is also a contrast of offers. The Rabshakeh promises a vine, a fig tree and a cistern if the people will 'come out' to him, and the promise ends in exile. Jesus says, 'Come to Me, all you who are weary and burdened, and I will give you rest,' Matthew 11:28, and His rest does not end in captivity. The false shepherd offers peace on his own terms. The true one gives it at His own cost.

A guard is needed. The narrative nowhere describes the angel as Christ, and a direct identification is not warranted from this text. The Christological reading rests on the Davidic covenant and on the pattern of the LORD's own deliverance that the New Testament sees completed in Jesus.
study.god:
The central question of the narrative is whether the LORD is able, and the answer comes in three movements. The first is that He is the living God who hears. The Rabshakeh's whole case is that the LORD is a name on a list of defeated gods. Hezekiah's reply begins with a title, 'LORD of Hosts, God of Israel, enthroned above the cherubim,' and a claim: 'You alone are God over all the kingdoms of the earth. You made the heavens and the earth,' 37:16. That is a doctrine of creation used as a weapon against a theology of power. The one who made everything cannot be a regional deity, and the empires that the Rabshakeh cites are among the things He made.

The second movement is that God hears prayer and answers by acting in His own way. Hezekiah asks for deliverance 'so that all the kingdoms of the earth may know,' which is a prayer for the LORD's glory more than for the king's safety. God agrees with the priority. He says He will save the city 'for My own sake,' 37:35, and that is not self-regard in a bad sense. It is the recognition that He is the only fit object of the world's worship, and that His glory and His people's good are bound together.

The third movement is that He holds together His freedom and His faithfulness. In the poem of 37:26 He says He planned the Assyrian rise long ago, so that Sennacherib is an instrument in His hand, Isaiah 10:5 to 15. Yet the king is fully responsible for the pride with which he swings the axe. This is how Scripture talks about providence: God rules, and human arrogance is real and answerable. It is in the same movement that He says, 'I know your sitting down, your going out and coming in,' which is the picture of a God who is neither absent nor surprised.

The chapter also shows His patience and His attention. He answers a taunting letter, and He does so not only with force but with words: Isaiah's message to Hezekiah gives the reason for the deliverance and a sign for the future, 37:30. God does not simply act, He explains, so that His people can know why and trust.

For worship, the narrative shapes how believers pray. It teaches us to bring the actual threatening letter, the real diagnosis or bill or accusation, and put it before Him as it is, and to ask for what will make His name known. It also asks for the courage of a quiet people on a wall who are told to say nothing, 36:21, because they have a king who has gone to pray. The confident, silent trust of Jerusalem's people is itself a form of worship, and the God who answered Hezekiah is the God who has promised to hear all who come to Him in the name of the Son.

crossReferences.note: The parallel account, almost word for word, with the addition of Hezekiah's tribute in 2 Kings 18:14 to 16. Comparing the two shows what Isaiah's book chooses to emphasise: the confrontation of faith and the vindication of the LORD, not the political details of the payment.

The LORD sends Isaiah to meet Ahaz at the end of the aqueduct of the upper pool, on the road to the Launderer's Field, with the message 'Do not be afraid.' The Rabshakeh stands in the same place. Ahaz was told not to fear and did not believe; Hezekiah hears the same word in 37:6 and believes.

The LORD calls Assyria the rod of His anger and then says He will punish its king for boasting of his own strength. The poem of 37:22 to 29 returns to that boast, showing that the pride of Sennacherib was already named and judged as Isaiah's first warnings.

As a lion growls over its prey and is not frightened by shepherds, so the LORD of Hosts will come down to fight on Mount Zion, and like birds hovering, He will shield Jerusalem and deliver it. The promise before the siege is fulfilled in the siege: the LORD fights without Judah's help.

The psalm calls God a refuge and strength and a help in trouble, pictures nations in uproar and kingdoms falling, and confesses that the LORD of Hosts is with His people. The psalm speaks the confidence that the deliverance of Jerusalem displayed, so it serves as the congregation's song of what Hezekiah's prayer secured.

At midnight the LORD struck down every firstborn in Egypt, and Pharaoh rose in the night, for there was a great cry in Egypt. The night strike on the camp in Isaiah 37:36, with the people waking to find the dead, reproduces the Passover pattern of salvation by the LORD's own act, not by the people's weapons.

The promise to David that his throne will be established forever. When the LORD says in Isaiah 37:35 that He will save the city for the sake of David, He is pointing to this covenant, which is the reason the house of David survives even a king as weak as Ahaz and a crisis as grave as this one.

'I am the LORD, and there is no other; there is no God but Me.' The LORD says this so that people from east to west will know there is none besides Him. It is the full statement of the faith that Hezekiah confesses in 37:16 and 37:20, and which the Rabshakeh's list of defeated gods denies.

We have a great High Priest, Jesus the Son of God, and are invited to approach the throne of grace with confidence to receive mercy and find grace in time of need. Hezekiah's act of spreading the letter in the temple is a shadow of this free access, now available through Christ.

God exalted Jesus and gave Him the name above every name, so that every knee should bow and every tongue confess that Jesus Christ is Lord. This answers the Rabshakeh's question 'Who among all the gods?' and fulfils Hezekiah's prayer that all the kingdoms of the earth will know that the LORD alone is God.

study.oneStory:
Isaiah 36 and 37 take a recurring problem in the Bible's story and show the pattern of its solution in miniature. Since Genesis 3 the line of the promised seed has been threatened. The serpent's offspring, in one guise after another, rise against it. Pharaoh drowns the infants, Haman plots against the Jews, Herod slaughters the boys of Bethlehem. Sennacherib is one of these threats, and he is the one who gets closest to the throne of David. If Jerusalem had fallen in 701, the line of David would have been cut off with the city. The story of salvation hangs, here, on a siege.

What the narrative answers from earlier in the story is the question of whether God will keep the promise to David. The covenant of 2 Samuel 7 had said the throne would endure, and the kings had done almost everything possible to put it at risk. Ahaz had trusted Assyria and sold the temple's silver, 2 Kings 16:7 to 8. Hezekiah, his son, now shows what a king looks like who trusts the LORD instead, and the contrast between the two meetings at the same aqueduct, one in chapter 7 and one in chapter 36, is the point. The promise holds in spite of the faithless, and it is received by the faithful.

What it sets up is chapters 38 to 39, where the reverse side is shown. Hezekiah is healed, then flatters Babylon's envoys, and the prophet announces the exile. So the very next scenes demonstrate that even this good king cannot be the one who saves the story. The deliverance of 701 BC is a brief, bright pledge in a darkening sky. After it, the book turns to comfort for exiles and to the Servant who will accomplish what no king could.

The ending of the whole Bible gives the full picture. The beast gathers the kings of the earth for battle against the rider on the white horse, and they are defeated by the sword from His mouth, Revelation 19:19 to 21, without one of the saints lifting a weapon. The final city is not saved by the army of the saints but by the Lamb, and its enemies are ended by His word. Hezekiah's silent wall, the unfired arrow, the dead camp at dawn, and the poem of the hook in the nose are early notes of the last chord, in which the LORD saves His people for His own sake, and the nations learn that He alone is God.

quiz.q: What is the central taunt the Rabshakeh presses on Judah in chapter 36?

options.text: That their trust, whether in Egypt or in the LORD, is misplaced and cannot save them from Assyria.
options.note: The Rabshakeh's speech repeatedly circles the question of trust, mocking both Egypt and the LORD as unable to deliver.

options.text: That Judah's army is too large for Assyria to defeat honestly.
options.note: The opposite; the Rabshakeh mocks Judah's military weakness, not its strength.

options.text: That Hezekiah's religious reforms were too generous to foreigners.
options.note: Not the substance of the taunt, which concerns misplaced trust and Assyria's overwhelming power, not foreign policy toward outsiders.

options.text: That Assyria secretly fears Jerusalem's defenses.
options.note: The opposite; the Rabshakeh presents Assyria as supremely confident and Jerusalem as helpless.

quiz.q: How does Hezekiah respond upon hearing the Rabshakeh's report in 37:1?

options.text: He tears his clothes, puts on sackcloth, and enters the house of the LORD.
options.note: Verse 1 describes exactly this response of grief and prayer rather than panic or retaliation.

options.text: He immediately surrenders the city to avoid bloodshed.
options.note: The opposite; Hezekiah turns to prayer and seeks the LORD's help, not surrender.

options.text: He orders the immediate execution of the Assyrian messengers.
options.note: Not Hezekiah's response; he commands silence and then turns to prayer.

options.text: He seeks a new military alliance with a foreign power.
options.note: The opposite of his response here; he seeks the LORD directly rather than another human alliance.

quiz.q: What does Hezekiah do with Sennacherib's threatening letter in 37:14?

options.text: He spreads it out before the LORD in the temple and prays.
options.note: Verse 14 describes exactly this act of bringing the letter directly before God in prayer.

options.text: He burns the letter without reading it.
options.note: The opposite; he reads it and then brings it before the LORD rather than destroying it unread.

options.text: He sends a written reply agreeing to Assyria's terms.
options.note: Not what happens; Hezekiah seeks the LORD rather than negotiating surrender.

options.text: He hides the letter from his officials and the prophet Isaiah.
options.note: The opposite; the crisis is shared with Isaiah, and the letter is brought openly before the LORD.

quiz.q: For whose sake does the LORD say He will defend Jerusalem in 37:35?

options.text: For His own sake and for the sake of His servant David.
options.note: Verse 35 states this explicitly, tying the deliverance to God's glory and His covenant with David.

options.text: For the sake of Judah's military achievements.
options.note: The opposite; the deliverance is credited entirely to the LORD, not to Judah's own military accomplishments.

options.text: For the sake of a treaty Hezekiah made with Egypt.
options.note: The chapter mocks reliance on Egypt rather than crediting it as the basis for deliverance.

options.text: For the sake of the wealth Hezekiah had accumulated.
options.note: Not the stated reason; the LORD names His own name and His covenant with David, not Hezekiah's wealth.

quiz.q: How does the LORD deliver Jerusalem from the Assyrian army in 37:36?

options.text: The angel of the LORD strikes down 185,000 men in the Assyrian camp in a single night.
options.note: Verse 36 describes exactly this act of direct divine deliverance without human military engagement.

options.text: Judah's army defeats Assyria in open battle.
options.note: The opposite; the text emphasizes that Judah did not need to fight, since the LORD acted alone.

options.text: Egypt's army arrives to rescue Jerusalem.
options.note: Egypt's help was mocked earlier as unreliable; the deliverance comes from the LORD alone, not Egypt.

options.text: Sennacherib voluntarily withdraws out of respect for Hezekiah.
options.note: The withdrawal follows the LORD's direct act of judgment on the army, not a voluntary change of heart.

questions: The Rabshakeh's central question was, on whom does your trust really rest? Where is that same question being asked of you right now, in a threat, a diagnosis, or a financial pressure?

Hezekiah took the enemy's blasphemous letter and spread it out before the LORD rather than trying to answer it in his own strength. What are you carrying today that you need to lay before God rather than manage alone?
The people were commanded to remain silent rather than answer the Rabshakeh's taunts. Where might silence and prayer serve you better than an immediate defensive answer?

The LORD acted alone, without a single Judean weapon raised, so that all the kingdoms of the earth would know He alone is God. Where in your life might God be asking you to step back and let Him act rather than striving in your own strength?

God delivered Jerusalem for His own name and for the sake of His covenant with David, a promise that runs forward to Christ. How does knowing God keeps His covenant promises across centuries strengthen your confidence in the promises He has made to you in Christ?

translationNotes.note: Rabshakeh is a title, chief cupbearer or field commander, not a personal name, referring to a senior Assyrian officer sent to deliver Sennacherib's ultimatum.

The murder of Sennacherib by his own sons is independently confirmed in Babylonian records, occurring roughly twenty years after this siege, showing the LORD's word of judgment against him was fulfilled in full.

The number 185,000 is given without further explanation of the means; ancient historians such as Herodotus preserve independent traditions of a disaster striking Assyrian forces in this campaign, though Scripture attributes the act directly to the angel of the LORD.
